newsitem.title: UK: Sterling pauses for breath, eyes 3.0 marks.
newsitem.headline: Sterling pauses for breath, eyes 3.0 marks.

text.p: Sterling paused for breath on Wednesday, setting its sight firmly on the 3.0-mark level, after a staggering two-day slide knocked it over eight pfennigs lower.
"The sell-off was a bit like a shower. Sterling had a knock-back but the sun is out and the umbrella is back down," said a trader at a European bank.

At 0930 GMT, sterling/mark was at 2.9910/20 up from 2.9826/36 late Europe on Tuesday. Still, it was off its early highs near 3.0033 marks, which is now acting as resistance, said traders. Cable was at $1.6272/82 against $1.6282/92 in late Europe as dollar/yen gained ground.
Sterling slumped this week from a high of 3.0627 marks on Monday to a low of 2.9735 marks on Tuesday. Against the dollar, it slid from $1.6640 to $1.6230 on Tuesday.

"We had quite a violent correction downwards in the last couple of days...I regard it as a bull-market correction and I don't think we have necessarily seen the top yet," said Ian Amstad, economist at Bankers Trust.
Analysts, moreover, see the fundamentals that spurred sterling/mark to 3.0878 last week -- its highest level since August 1989 -- remaining.
"Sterling will remain well underpinned," said the trader.

Sterling, which has climbed from as low as 2.2755 in August 1996, has been spirited higher by a cocktail of factors including strong domestic growth, higher interest rates and its status as a haven currency if a broad EMU is launched.
"We are a country with an aggressive central bank and with the highest-yielding currency in the G7," said Amstad.
With this in mind, and the economy showing little signs of slowing, Amstad said sterling remains attractive.
"We need to see signs of the economy slowing before sterling comes off. It looks like we are going to see strong numbers for a few months yet, with the currency underpinned," he added.

The market is now focusing on the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee meeting next week to see if the central bank will raise rates. Data showing a record rise in personal credit in June, for instance, highlight, the need for higher rates, some analysts said.
"Rates are going higher," said the trader at the European bank. "If not next week, then in September."
The BoE has raised interest rates three times since May 1. The UK, with rates of 6.75 percent, now offers one of the highest rates in the European Union.
Short-sterling futures contract, for instance, imply that three-month rates, currently just over 7.0 percent, will be at 7.25 percent by September.
Meantime, cable was undermined as the dollar firmed in Europe, topping 1.84 marks. Dollar/Swiss was also firm and eyeing 47-month peaks set on Monday.
The German mark was firmer on most its European crosses, its sentiment boosted by speculation the Bundesbank may alter its money market policy to allow German rates to head higher.
